pieces.desc: Steps one square forward. Can only catch diagonally forward.
pieces.history: The foot soldier (padati in Sanskrit, baidaq in Arabic). The two-square first step, and capturing en passant, were added in Europe in the late Middle Ages to speed the game up.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square straight (forward only), to move; one square diagonally (forward only), to capture. Captures a different way from how it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Leaps exactly three squares diagonally, over anything.
pieces.origin: A plain leaper of fairy chess problems, the (3,3) jump.
pieces.history: The (3,3) leaper: ferz (1,1), alfil (2,2), tripper (3,3). It can reach only one square in eight of the board.
pieces.patent: Leaps: three squares diagonally. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Travels along any line but must hop over the first thing in its way, landing just beyond it. No hurdle, no move.
pieces.origin: Invented by T. R. Dawson, 1912.
pieces.history: Invented in 1912 by Thomas Rayner Dawson, the English problemist who did more than anyone to make fairy chess a field of its own. It is one of the oldest and best-loved fairy pieces: it can only move by hopping over something.
pieces.patent: Hops: straight, over the first thing in the way, landing just beyond it; diagonally, over the first thing in the way, landing just beyond it. Captures the way it moves. Needs something to hop over.

pieces.desc: Leaps exactly two squares diagonally, over anything.
pieces.origin: "The elephant" of shatranj, the medieval ancestor of the bishop.
pieces.history: The elephant of shatranj, which jumped exactly two squares diagonally. Around 1475 to 1500 Europe replaced it with the long-range bishop, but the old elephant lives on in fairy chess under its Arabic name.
pieces.patent: Leaps: two squares diagonally. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance straight forward, and only forward.
pieces.origin: The kyōsha, "incense chariot", of shogi.
pieces.history: The kyōsha, "incense chariot", of shogi: it slides any distance straight forward, and can never come back.
pieces.patent: Slides: any distance straight (forward only). Captures the way it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Leaps exactly three squares up, down, left or right, over anything.
pieces.origin: A plain leaper of fairy chess problems, the (3,0) jump.
pieces.history: The (3,0) leaper, one of the simple jumps fairy chess lists by size: wazir (1,0), dabbaba (2,0), threeleaper (3,0).
pieces.patent: Leaps: three squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Leaps three one way and two to the side, over anything.
pieces.history: A three-and-two leaper. A modern fairy piece, named in the habit of naming leapers after animals; it has no great history of its own beyond the problem books.
pieces.patent: Leaps: a wide L (three and two). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Leaps exactly two squares up, down, left or right, over anything.
pieces.origin: The war engine (dabbaba, a covered siege machine) of Tamerlane chess, 14th century.
pieces.history: The war engine of Tamerlane chess, the dabbaba: a covered siege machine that crept up to walls. As a piece it jumps exactly two squares straight.
pieces.patent: Leaps: two squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Steps one square diagonally.
pieces.origin: The counsellor of shatranj, the ancestor of the queen.
pieces.history: The counsellor of shatranj (fers, from the Persian farzin): one step diagonally. It sat beside the shah, and it is the piece that became the queen. Fairy chess keeps the old name for the old move.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square diagonally. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: A long knight: leaps three one way and one to the side, over anything.
pieces.origin: From Tamerlane chess.
pieces.history: A long knight, three and one. It appears in Tamerlane chess, the great medieval game associated with Timur's court in the fourteenth century, and in other large historical variants; fairy chess kept the name for the move.
pieces.patent: Leaps: a long L (three and one). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Moves like a knight, but one straight step first. Anything on that first square blocks it.
pieces.origin: The horse of xiangqi.
pieces.history: The horse of xiangqi. It moves like a knight but in two steps, one straight and one diagonal, so a piece on the first square blocks it. "Mao" is the fairy chess name, from the Chinese ma, horse.
pieces.patent: Leaps: a knight’s L (two and one). Captures the way it moves. Can be blocked on the way.

pieces.desc: Steps one square straight forward or straight back, or one square diagonally forward. Never sideways.
pieces.origin: From chu shogi, the larger shogi of medieval Japan.
pieces.history: The copper general of chu shogi, the larger shogi played in Japan from about the fourteenth century: a weaker cousin of the silver.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square straight (forward or back only); one square diagonally (forward only). Captures the way it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Steps one square up, down, left or right.
pieces.origin: Named for the vizier.
pieces.history: Wazir is the Arabic for vizier. Tamerlane chess had a vizier that stepped one square straight; fairy chess uses the name for that move.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square straight. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Slides like a bishop, but can only catch by jumping exactly one thing on the way.
pieces.origin: The cannon (pao) of xiangqi turned diagonal, from 20th-century variants.
pieces.history: The cannon's diagonal twin: it slides like a bishop, and captures only by jumping exactly one piece. It turns up in modern variants of xiangqi and in fairy chess.
pieces.patent: Slides and hops: any distance diagonally, to move; any distance diagonally, but over exactly one thing first, to capture. Captures only by hopping over something. Needs something to hop over.

pieces.desc: Hops twice each turn: one square in any direction, then another, so it can turn a corner. It never takes anything. It can hop onto the head of a piece of its own side and ride there; taking that piece takes the rabbit too.
pieces.origin: Grove Chess’s own, 2026.
pieces.history: Grove Chess's own, from the rabbits that have always lived in the grove (2026). It has no fairy chess record: no other game lets a piece climb onto a friend's head and ride.

pieces.desc: Steps one square diagonally, or one square straight forward. It cannot step sideways or straight back.
pieces.origin: From shogi, Japanese chess, where pieces are wedges that point at the enemy; this one has been in the game since about the 1100s.
pieces.history: A silver general of shogi, Japanese chess. Shogi pieces are flat wedges that point at the enemy, the same colour for both sides, and a captured piece can be dropped back in on the other side. The silver steps diagonally or straight forward.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square diagonally; one square straight (forward only). Captures the way it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Goes one or two squares diagonally, leaping over anything on the way.
pieces.origin: The ferz and alfil together, the elephant of several modern variants (sometimes called the modern elephant).
pieces.history: The old elephant (the alfil) with the counsellor's step added. Several modern variants call this piece the elephant, a guess at what the shatranj elephant might have been if it could also take one step.
pieces.patent: Steps and leaps: one square diagonally; two squares diagonally. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Leaps exactly two squares in any of the eight directions, over anything, and never anywhere nearer.
pieces.origin: The alfil and dabbaba together, named in fairy chess catalogues.
pieces.history: Every square exactly two away in a straight line or a diagonal. A name from the fairy chess catalogues, where compounds of simple leapers are given names of their own.
pieces.patent: Leaps: two squares diagonally; two squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Jumps in an L, two one way and one to the side, over anything.
pieces.history: The horse of chaturanga. Its L-shaped jump is the one move in chess that has never changed: the same in India fifteen hundred years ago, in shatranj, in medieval Europe and today.
pieces.patent: Leaps: a knight’s L (two and one). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything.

pieces.desc: Steps one square straight in any direction, or one square diagonally forward. It cannot step diagonally back.
pieces.origin: From shogi, Japanese chess.
pieces.history: The gold general of shogi: it guards the king, stepping anywhere but diagonally back. In shogi most pieces that cross into the far camp promote to move like a gold.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square straight; one square diagonally (forward only). Captures the way it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Steps one square in any direction but sideways.
pieces.origin: From chu shogi.
pieces.history: The ferocious leopard of chu shogi: one step in any direction but sideways.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square diagonally; one square straight (forward or back only). Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance diagonally.
pieces.history: It began as the elephant (al-fil in shatranj), which jumped exactly two squares diagonally: the alfil, also in this game. With the queen, around 1475 to 1500, it became the long-range bishop. Other languages see it differently: in French it is the fool (fou), in German the runner (Läufer).
pieces.patent: Slides: any distance diagonally. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Steps one square diagonally, or leaps exactly three squares straight, over anything.
pieces.origin: The ferz and threeleaper together, named in fairy chess catalogues.
pieces.history: The ferz and the threeleaper in one. A name from the fairy chess catalogues.
pieces.patent: Steps and leaps: one square diagonally; three squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Steps one square in any direction but straight forward.
pieces.origin: From chu shogi, where it cannot see what is in front of it.
pieces.history: The blind tiger of chu shogi: one step in any direction but straight ahead, which, being blind, it cannot see.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square diagonally; one square straight (sideways or backward only). Captures the way it moves. Has a forward.

pieces.desc: Steps one square diagonally, or leaps exactly two squares straight, over anything.
pieces.origin: From chu shogi, named for the kirin, a beast of East Asian legend.
pieces.history: The kirin of chu shogi, named for the kirin (qilin), a hoofed, horned beast of East Asian legend. In chu shogi it promotes to the lion, the game's great piece.
pieces.patent: Steps and leaps: one square diagonally; two squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Steps one square straight, or leaps exactly two squares diagonally, over anything.
pieces.origin: From chu shogi.
pieces.history: The phoenix of chu shogi, the kirin's partner: where the kirin steps diagonally and leaps straight, the phoenix steps straight and leaps diagonally. It promotes to the queen.
pieces.patent: Steps and leaps: one square straight; two squares diagonally. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance up or down, and steps one square left or right.
pieces.origin: The vertical mover (kengyō) of chu shogi, the larger shogi of medieval Japan.
pieces.history: Timothy's name (2026). The move is the vertical mover (kengyō) of chu shogi: it slides any distance up and down the board and steps one square to either side. Chu shogi promotes it to the flying ox.
pieces.patent: Slides and steps: any distance straight (forward or back only); one square straight (sideways only). Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Slides like a rook, but can only catch by jumping exactly one thing on the way.
pieces.origin: From xiangqi, Chinese chess.
pieces.history: The cannon of xiangqi, Chinese chess, which took its modern form around the Song dynasty (960 to 1279). It moves like a chariot but captures by jumping exactly one piece. Its character was first written with the stone radical, a catapult, and later with the fire radical, a gun.
pieces.patent: Slides and hops: any distance straight, to move; any distance straight, but over exactly one thing first, to capture. Captures only by hopping over something. Needs something to hop over.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance left or right, and steps one square up or down.
pieces.origin: The side mover (ōgyō) of chu shogi, the larger shogi of medieval Japan.
pieces.history: Timothy's name (2026). The move is the side mover (ōgyō) of chu shogi, the larger shogi played in Japan from about the fourteenth century: it slides any distance across the board and steps one square forward or back. Chu shogi promotes it to the free boar.
pieces.patent: Slides and steps: any distance straight (sideways only); one square straight (forward or back only). Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: A knight that keeps going: repeats the same L jump in a straight line until something stops it.
pieces.origin: T. R. Dawson, 1925.
pieces.history: Also T. R. Dawson, 1925: a knight that keeps going, repeating its jump in a straight line. A favourite of chess problem composers ever since.
pieces.patent: Slides: knight’s Ls, again and again in a line. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Steps one square in any direction.
pieces.history: The raja of chaturanga, the Indian game of about the sixth century that chess grew from, then the shah of Persian and Arabic shatranj. "Checkmate" is the Persian shah mat, usually read as "the king is helpless". Its move has hardly changed in fifteen hundred years; castling was added in late medieval Europe.
pieces.patent: Steps: one square straight; one square diagonally. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Steps one square straight, or leaps exactly two squares straight, over anything. A rook that cannot go far.
pieces.origin: The wazir and dabbaba together, a short-range rook from Ralph Betza’s Chess with Different Armies.
pieces.history: A short-range rook: one step or a two-square leap, straight. It belongs to Ralph Betza's Chess with Different Armies (1990s), where each side can field a different army of equal strength.
pieces.patent: Steps and leaps: one square straight; two squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance up, down, left or right.
pieces.history: The chariot: ratha in chaturanga, rukh in Persian, and from that the English word. Its move, straight lines as far as it likes, has stayed the same since the beginning. Its castle shape came later, in Europe.
pieces.patent: Slides: any distance straight. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Makes knight jumps that curve, each one turning further, tracing a circle. Stops at anything in its path.
pieces.history: A modern fairy piece: a knight that keeps going, but turning a little each jump, so its path curves round a circle. It is named for the shape that path draws.
pieces.patent: Circles: knight’s Ls that turn round a circle. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: Leaps to any square exactly two away, over anything.
pieces.history: A modern fairy piece that can reach every square exactly two away: the dabbaba, the alfil and the knight in one. Named, like many leapers, after an animal.
pieces.patent: Leaps: a knight’s L (two and one); two squares diagonally; two squares straight. Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: A bishop that can also jump like a knight.
pieces.origin: From Capablanca chess, 1920s.
pieces.history: Bishop and knight together. Pietro Carrera called it the centaur in his large chess of 1617; Henry Bird used it in 1874; José Raúl Capablanca, world champion, put it in his ten-file chess in the 1920s, and Capablanca's name, the archbishop, is the one that stuck.
pieces.patent: Slides and leaps: any distance diagonally; a knight’s L (two and one). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: A rook that can also jump like a knight.
pieces.origin: From Capablanca chess, the 1920s; earlier, as the "champion" and "marshal", in variants back to the 1600s.
pieces.history: Rook and knight together. Carrera's champion of 1617, Bird's guard of 1874, and Capablanca's chancellor of the 1920s. Computer studies put it, and the archbishop, at nearly the worth of a queen.
pieces.patent: Slides and leaps: any distance straight; a knight’s L (two and one). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

pieces.desc: Slides any distance in a straight line or a diagonal.
pieces.history: For most of its life a weak piece: the counsellor (mantri in India, farzin or fers in Persia and the Arab world) who stepped one square diagonally. Around 1475 to 1500, in Spain and Italy, it became the queen and gained its huge move, the change that made modern chess. Players at the time called the new game "mad queen" chess.
pieces.patent: Slides: any distance straight; any distance diagonally. Captures the way it moves.

pieces.desc: A queen that can also jump like a knight. The strongest piece here.
pieces.origin: The queen of some 18th-century Russian chess, and the maharaja of the Indian game "The Maharajah and the Sepoys".
pieces.history: Queen and knight together, the strongest piece in common use. Some regional Russian chess of the 1700s let the queen move this way, and it is the lone maharaja of the old Indian game "The Maharajah and the Sepoys".
pieces.patent: Slides and leaps: any distance straight; any distance diagonally; a knight’s L (two and one). Captures the way it moves. Jumps over anything on its leaps.

groups.ask: One match or a series, and what ends it?

fields.label: A session is
fields.help: One level: play it, then another. A descent: level after level, harder each time down, until every piece you have is gone. A golf course: hole after hole, strokes against par. Autochess rounds: set up, watch, and keep going while you have lives.

fields.label: Each level
fields.help: Rolling at random keeps only the difficulty, the pieces you allow, and the rule that it must be winnable and balanced. Rolling like the daily also insists on a high skill ceiling.

fields.label: Out of moves
fields.help: For a descent. Losing every piece always ends it.

fields.label: Lives
fields.help: For autochess rounds: a lost round costs one.

fields.label: Course
fields.help: Each course has its own holes, balls and ground. The title screen offers the ones you have opened: finishing a course opens the next.

fields.label: Play a chess variant
fields.help: A real chess variant from its starting position, against the thinking side (Timothy, 2026-10-11). The board, the pieces and the rules are the variant’s; the settings that still matter are how they think and the move limit.

fields.label: Ground
fields.help: Crumbling: every square you move a piece off falls away. Shrinking: every few moves a square on the edge drops into the dark and the board closes in, at random or round in a spiral.

fields.label: The edge falls every
fields.help: Only for shrinking ground.

fields.label: Magic edges
fields.help: Like Pac-Man: off one edge is on at the other. Joined edges glow. A piece that slides all the way round comes back to where it started, so it stops there; a ball rolling round with nothing to stop it arrives back where it began, which is no move.

fields.label: Geared
fields.help: After every turn the board turns a quarter turn clockwise, with everything on it. Your pieces turn with it, so they move as ever; the rabbits’ patterns do not, so a rabbit that hops up the screen goes a different way across the board each turn. Square boards only.

fields.label: Statues
fields.help: Standing stones, each with a spiral cut in it, in the middle of the board. They never move and nothing can take them. Sliders stop at them, leapers jump them, and the grasshopper and the cannon can hop over them.

fields.label: A row of statues that opens
fields.help: The middle row is all statues (in place of the count above), and after every turn one of them, at random, sinks away and opens its square (Timothy, 2026-10-12).

fields.label: Statues can be taken
fields.help: Statues are neutral pieces (Timothy, 2026-10-13): they never move or do anything, but either side can take one, and then it is gone. Sliders stop at them; leapers and hoppers go over them. Off: nothing can take them, the first way. Golf keeps them off.

fields.label: A row of ghosts in front of each side
fields.help: Ghosts fill the row in front of each side, where pawns stand in chess (Timothy, 2026-10-13). A ghost never moves and never takes. Its own side moves through it as if it were not there, and once one of them passes through or onto it, it is gone for good. The other side cannot pass it or land on it, though a leaper can jump over. So at first neither side can reach the other: you open your own wall as you go.

fields.label: Gates
fields.help: Gates between the two sides, up one turn and down the next (Timothy, 2026-10-13). Down, a gate is open ground; up, nothing passes it and nothing can stand there. A gate with a piece on it stays down until the piece leaves.

fields.label: Wandering clouds
fields.help: Clouds that drift a square a turn, any way, on their own (Timothy, 2026-10-13). A piece under a cloud is hidden from the other side, and so is its move into the cloud. A move that runs into a hidden piece stops there and takes it. You always see your own pieces, cloud or not.

fields.label: A cloud on the second rows, first turn
fields.help: For the first turn, a cloud covers the row in front of each side. Each side moves through its own cloud freely; the other side’s stops it (a piece can step in, not past), and nothing in a cloud can be taken by the other side. So nobody can take anything on the first move. It lifts once both sides have moved (Timothy, 2026-10-10 and 11: with no second row of pawns, this protects the Kings at the start).

fields.label: Each cloud stops only the other side
fields.help: On: your pieces go through your own cloud as if it were not there, and only theirs stops you (and the same for them). Off: both clouds stop everyone, the first version.

groups.ask: What does each side have, and where does it stand?

fields.label: A full row each
fields.help: Each side starts with as many pieces as the board is wide: six on a six by six board, yours and theirs (Timothy, 2026-10-10). Off: the counts set below, under Yours and Theirs.

fields.label: Line up like chess
fields.help: Your pieces start in a line along the bottom edge, theirs along the top. Off: scattered within the rows below.

fields.label: Stand in the order given
fields.help: For a run, whose sides are given rather than dealt (the descent): both lines stand in the order they were given, file by file, facing each other like chess, in the middle of the row. Off: where each piece stands is part of the dice roll.

fields.label: Pieces to start with
fields.help: For a descent and autochess rounds.

fields.label: You start with
fields.help: Dealt from these.

fields.label: Always dealt a King
fields.help: With a royal King: if the deal has none, your first piece becomes one.

fields.label: Start within the bottom
fields.help: When not lined up.

fields.label: Lay out your pieces first
fields.help: Before the first move, put your pieces where you like in your first two rows (Timothy, 2026-10-10). Nowhere that lets either side take a piece on its first move. Par is worked out again for your layout.

fields.label: Their line
fields.help: For a descent with one upgrade a board, where both sides start with "You start with". The same files: their first piece stands opposite your first, like Microchess. Reversed (Timothy, 2026-10-13): their line is yours read the other way, so each side, looking from its own end, has the same piece on its left.

options.label: The same files as yours, like Microchess
Yours reversed, as if turned round the board

fields.label: Pieces
fields.help: Dark versions of chess and fairy pieces.

fields.label: Mirror your pieces instead
fields.help: They get a copy of your hand, facing you, like chess.

fields.label: Start within the top
fields.help: Loose rabbits and the hole start up there too, lined up or not.

fields.label: Free rabbits
fields.help: Rabbits loose on the board, on top of the ones inside their pieces.

fields.label: Rabbits eat your pieces
fields.help: Off: a rabbit that would land on one of your pieces waits instead.

fields.label: Balls on a course
fields.help: Each hole uses one, in turn. Sticky stops beside the first thing it passes; a ghost rolls straight through pieces.

fields.label: The ball moves
fields.help: On ice: up, down, left or right, and it rolls until something stops it. Like a putt: up, down, left or right, as far as you like. Like a billiard ball: diagonally, as far as you like, bouncing off the edges (the reflecting bishop from Billiards Chess). It never takes anything. Hit by the pieces: it never moves by itself; any piece, yours or theirs, that moves into it sends it sliding along the line of that move, like on ice, until something stops it. Sticky: like ice, but it stops beside the first thing it passes. A ghost: like ice, straight through pieces.

fields.label: The ball captures
fields.help: On: rolling or sliding into one of their pieces, the ball takes it and stops there. Off: it stops short, and never takes anything.

groups.ask: Who moves each side, and when?

fields.label: Who moves your pieces
fields.help: Autochess: before the game you put rabbits you have caught into your pieces, choose which way each faces and the order of your line. Then it plays itself: each rabbit picks the way, its piece picks how, the same as theirs.

fields.label: Your rabbits
fields.help: For autochess. Caught: one rabbit for every time you caught its kind, in the descent or the daily.

fields.label: Waiting allowed
fields.help: Off: you must move a piece every turn (Timothy, 2026-10-10). A side with no move at all still passes.

fields.label: Moved by
fields.help: A rabbit inside: each piece is possessed by a rabbit, whose pattern decides which way it goes each turn (left, up, a pause); the piece’s own moves decide how. One rabbit leads them (2026-10-13): their pieces think, and a single Rabbit, starting on their King, sets how: its trait is their mood (aggressive and hunter hunt, shy flees) and its intelligence how far ahead they look. It hops every turn by its own mind.

fields.label: Thinking skill
fields.help: For pieces of theirs that think, and thinking rabbits.

fields.label: Kinds of rabbit inside
fields.help: One kind: every piece moves to the same pattern (or has the same trait), so you can see it. More: each piece may have its own.

fields.label: They move one piece a turn
fields.help: Like you. A piece that can take one of yours goes; otherwise their pieces take turns, in order. Off: every piece of theirs moves every turn. Loose rabbits always hop.

fields.label: They may stay put
fields.help: Off: when they move one piece a turn, a piece of theirs always moves; if the one whose turn it is would rather stay, it moves anyway, and if it cannot, the next one goes. On: a rabbit may choose to stay where it is.

fields.label: Rabbits move by
fields.help: A mind: every rabbit, loose or inside a piece, picks its own move each turn, by its trait and its intelligence. A fixed pattern: the old way, a hidden pattern that repeats.

fields.label: Intelligence
fields.help: For rabbits with minds. Low: fumbling, half blind to danger. High: sharp, sees what you could take, never boxes itself in.

fields.label: Traits
fields.help: Which kinds of mind can turn up. Aggressive goes for you; Hunter for your strongest piece; Shy keeps away; Guard stays with its own side; Messy is all over the place; Habit keeps a learnable pattern but steps round trouble.

fields.label: Rabbit patterns
fields.help: For free rabbits and the ones inside pieces. Every named kind has its own colour; "every named kind" adds three that pause.

fields.label: Kung fu: no turns
fields.help: Real time, after Kung-Fu Chess (2002): move any piece of yours whenever it is ready, and so do they. A move takes time to travel, so a piece can dodge, and a piece that has moved rests before it moves again. Take their King.

fields.label: Travel time a square
fields.help: Kung-Fu Chess’s lightning speed is 200; its standard speed is 1,000.

fields.label: Your pieces rest for
fields.help: Lightning is 2 seconds (20); standard is 10 seconds (100).

fields.label: Theirs rest for
fields.help: In a descent, their first level’s; they get quicker each level down.

fields.label: They start a move at most every
fields.help: Their side plays like one opponent: one move at a time, this often at most. In a descent, their first level’s; it shortens each level down.

groups.ask: How do you win, how do you lose, and what ends a game that stalls?

fields.label: How you win
fields.help: Catch them, then the ball: the hole stays shut until every possessed piece and loose rabbit is caught, then sink the ball in it. King and rabbit make sure they have one. Sink the ball gives you a ball and a moving hole. Mix picks capture, King or rabbit per layout.

fields.label: Your King is royal
fields.help: Lose the King, lose the game.

fields.label: The hole moves by
fields.help: Only when there is a hole. A hidden pattern, like a rabbit’s.

fields.label: Ball must stop on the hole
fields.help: Off: it drops in when it rolls over the hole. On: it has to come to rest there.

fields.label: Move limit
fields.help: 0 means no limit.

fields.label: Two left: the board closes in
fields.help: Once only one piece of yours and one of theirs are left, the edge falls away every move, round and inward, until they meet. A square with a piece on it never falls.

groups.ask: What changes between the games of a series?

fields.label: Finishing a level finds you something
fields.help: A new piece while you have room; once your hand is full, an upgrade: a suit, fusing two pieces, or a joker. Pieces of theirs you take are claimed, and can be combined with yours after the level.

fields.label: Between levels
fields.help: Find pieces, then upgrades: a new piece while you have room, then suits, fusing and jokers; pieces of theirs you take can be combined with yours. One upgrade a board, each side (Timothy, 2026-10-12): every new board you choose one of two, a piece to combine with one of yours or a suit for one, and they get one at random. They carry a lineup down as you do, and a Rabbit with it.

options.label: One upgrade a board, each side

fields.label: Pieces you can find
fields.help: What a run offers when it finds a piece. Pieces vetoed in the catalog are left out anyway.

fields.label: Jokers can turn up
fields.help: Rules for the rest of a run: Double Time, Foresight, Recruiter, Lazy Rabbits, Overtime.

fields.label: Spend acorns in a shop
fields.help: For autochess rounds. Each round earns acorns (three for a win, one for a loss, one per piece of theirs taken), spent between rounds on pieces and upgrades in place of a free pick.

fields.label: What you find carries over
fields.help: For a descent. Every piece you find joins your roster, and you can start a later descent with any of them. Going deeper lights waystones for good: at depth 4 every descent starts with an upgrade, at depth 7 with one more piece, at depth 10 with two upgrades.

fields.label: Waystones give upgrades at the start
fields.help: For a descent. Off (Timothy, 2026-10-10: "decent mode should give no upgrade when starting"): every descent starts with only its pieces. On: the waystones at depth 4 and 10 each give an upgrade of your choice before the first level.

fields.label: Fairy pieces from depth
fields.help: For a descent. Above this depth only classic pieces turn up, on either side and among what you find, so a new player first meets pieces whose moves they know (Timothy, 2026-10-10). 1: fairy pieces from the start.

fields.label: The board is 7 by 7 from depth
fields.help: For a descent with one upgrade a board. 0: never. From this depth the board is 7 by 7, and each side gets two more pieces to fill its row.

fields.label: The board grows
fields.help: For a descent. Off: every level is the board size set under Board (6 by 6). On: a row and a column more every few levels, up to 8 by 8.

groups.ask: How hard is it, how does it climb, and what must every level pass?

fields.label: First level’s difficulty
fields.help: For a descent. The first level is found at this difficulty (measured: a novice bot plays it two dozen times), and every level after aims a little higher, as fast as "It gets harder" says.

fields.label: It gets harder
fields.help: Each level down, or each round: a higher difficulty aimed at (gently 0.35 a level, steadily 0.6, steeply 1), more pieces of theirs and sharper rabbits.

fields.label: Difficulty
fields.help: Measured by a novice bot playing the level two dozen times (metrics.js): how often it loses, and how long the shortest win is. Needs the solver.

fields.label: Aim for difficulty
fields.help: A number in place of a band: the level must measure within one of it (1 aims at 1 to 2). 0 uses the band above. The descent sets this itself, level by level.

fields.label: Engaging, at least
fields.help: A first guess at how engaging a level is: choices that matter, pieces used, tension, comebacks. 0 lets anything through.

fields.label: Skill ceiling, at least
fields.help: How much faster an expert wins than a novice: 10 means twice as fast. A high ceiling is easy to win in many moves and hard to win in few. 0 lets anything through.

fields.label: Only deal winnable levels
fields.help: The solver plays each layout first and throws out any it cannot win in time. It also sets par.

fields.label: Balance rules
fields.help: On: no piece on either side can capture on its first move, every piece of yours can move at the start, and every strange piece (fairy pieces, and the grasshopper-like ones that need the right circumstances) has a job: it makes a catch in the winning line, or the level is worse without it. Strict: every piece has a job. Needs the solver.

groups.ask: What can each side see, and which hints show?

fields.label: Show where theirs can go
fields.help: A purple ring on every square their pieces’ moves cover, updating as pieces move: the squares that are dangerous to stand on (Timothy, 2026-10-10 and 11). It includes squares under their own pieces that another of theirs guards, and a pawn’s diagonals even when empty (2026-10-12).

fields.label: Show where yours can go
fields.help: A gold ring on every square one of your pieces could move to. Off by default (2026-10-11: "less useful and muddies the board"); tapping a piece still lights its own squares.

fields.label: Shields on guarded pieces
fields.help: A piece of yours that another of yours would avenge (if it were taken there, yours could take back on that square) wears a shield, which falls into place with a clink when it becomes guarded: silver for one guard, gold for two or more.

fields.label: Shields on squares you guard
fields.help: A flat shield on an empty square their pieces reach (a purple ring) that one of yours could take back on: move a piece there and it is guarded. Silver for one guard, gold for two or more. With a piece picked up, its own moves are tried for real: it cannot guard itself (Timothy, 2026-10-13).

fields.label: Beacons on what can be taken
fields.help: A beam of light rises from what could be taken next: purple from a piece of yours they could take on their next move if it stays (on your King, that is check), green from a piece of theirs you can take now (Timothy, 2026-10-11).

fields.label: Needles through pinned pieces
fields.help: A piece pinned to its King (it stands between its King and a piece of the other side, so moving it would leave the King to be taken) has a sewing needle driven down through it, which drops in from above when the pin starts (Timothy, 2026-10-13). Yours and theirs, wherever losing the King loses. The rules still let it move: moving it loses.

daily.name: The daily
daily.blurb: One board a day, the same for everyone: easy to win in a lot of moves, hard to win in a few.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: One game at a time, each rolled the way the daily is.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: Rolled: its size, its shape and everything on it.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Rolled with the board, a full row each, lined up like chess.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; one rabbit leads theirs: their pieces think, and its mind (intelligence 3 to 5) sets their mood. Turns, yours first.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Rolled with the board, with at least 18 moves.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: None: each game stands alone.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Aims at 4 of 10; each board searched to be winnable in 4 to 10 moves, balanced, engaging (at least 50 of 100) and with a high skill ceiling.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

descent.name: The descent
descent.blurb: Tall rook, bishop, King, knight and short rook each, a full row on a five by six board; theirs stand opposite, each piece facing its twin, as in chess. In front of each side stands a row of ghosts: yours let your pieces through and vanish as they pass, theirs stop you. One rabbit leads their side: its kind is how they play. Take their King to fall to the next board, where each side gets an upgrade: you choose one of two. From depth 6 the board is seven by seven. If they take your King the descent is over.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: A descent: board after board, deeper each time, until they take your King. Running out of moves drops you to the next board, with nothing found.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: 5 × 6 rectangle, with a row of ghosts in front of each side.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Yours: Tall rook, Bishop, King, Knight, Short rook, in that order. Theirs: the same, mirrored, each piece facing its twin. Lined up like chess.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; one rabbit leads them: their pieces think, and its mind (intelligence 3) sets their mood. Turns, yours first; one piece a side each turn.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Take their King; lose your King and you lose. A limit of 20 moves; with one piece left each, the board closes in.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: Each new board, both sides get an upgrade: you choose one of two (a piece to combine, or a suit), they get one at random; the board is 7 × 7 from depth 6 and fairy pieces from depth 4.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Not searched: each board is the two lines as they stand. What climbs is their rabbit’s intelligence, from 3, steadily, and the upgrades they get.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

kungfu.name: Kung fu descent
kungfu.blurb: The descent with no turns, after Kung-Fu Chess. Move any piece whenever it is ready, and so do they; moves take time to travel, and a piece that moved must rest. Take their King to fall to the next level.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: A descent: board after board, deeper each time, until they take your King. Running out of moves drops you to the next board, with nothing found.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: 6 × 6 square, with one statue either side can take.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Yours: 6 from Knight, Bishop, Rook, King. Theirs: a full row from King, Pawn, Knight, Bishop. Lined up like chess; you lay yours out first.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; a rabbit inside each of theirs picks its way, by its own mind (intelligence 3). No turns: any piece moves when it is ready, and theirs too.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Take their King; lose your King and you lose. No move limit.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: Finishing a board finds you a piece, up to 8, then upgrades and jokers; fairy pieces from depth 4 and what you find carries over to later descents.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Starts at 1 of 10 and climbs steadily, their pieces resting less each board; each board searched to be winnable in 3 to 10 moves and balanced.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

chaos.name: Chaos
chaos.blurb: A single level from a completely random mix of every rule and setting. It is always winnable and balanced, and as hard as you ask.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: One game at a time, each rolled completely at random.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: 6 × 6; its shape and everything on it rolled.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Rolled with the board, lined up like chess.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; how theirs move is rolled. Turns, yours first.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Take their King; lose your King and you lose. The move limit is rolled; with one piece left each, the board closes in.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: None: each game stands alone.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Normal (4 to 6); each board searched to be winnable and balanced.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

golf.name: Golf
golf.blurb: A course of holes. Your pieces are the walls, the ramps and, with some balls, the clubs; sink the ball in as few strokes as you can.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: A golf course: The Meadow, 6 holes, strokes against par.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: Each hole its own, 6 × 6 to start, changing as the course goes round.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Yours: 3 from Rook, Bishop, Knight, King, Wazir and 2 more, and a ball: putting and sticky. Theirs: none; one loose rabbit. Scattered in the first 2 rows; you lay yours out first.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; a loose rabbit hops by its own mind (intelligence 4). Turns, yours first; one piece a side each turn.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Sink the ball in as few strokes as you can. At most 15 strokes a hole.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: Nothing between holes; the course itself changes as it goes round.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Any difficulty; each hole searched to be winnable in 3 to 9 strokes and balanced.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

variants.name: Chess variants
variants.blurb: Real chess variants, small and strange, from their own starting positions, against a side that thinks. Pick one below.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: One game of Gardner minichess, from its own starting position.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: 5 × 5, the variant’s own board.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Yours: King, Queen, Rook, Knight, Bishop and 5 Pawns. Theirs: the same. As the variant stands them.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; they think two moves ahead. Turns, yours first; one piece a side each turn.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Take their King. No move limit.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: None: each game stands alone.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Not measured: it plays as it stands.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

trials.name: Piece trials
trials.blurb: A layout from the piece trials: the same army on each side, theirs thinking. Take their King and keep yours.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: One game, from a set position.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: The position’s own board.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: As the position stands them.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: You move yours; they think two moves ahead. Turns, yours first; one piece a side each turn.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Take their King; lose your King and you lose. No move limit.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: None: each game stands alone.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Not measured: it plays as it stands.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.

autochess.name: Autochess
autochess.blurb: Put rabbits in your pieces and let them fight. Win rounds to grow your side; lose three and it is over.

parts.name: Format
parts.text: Autochess rounds, until you have lost 3 lives.

parts.name: Board
parts.text: 6 × 6 square, with one statue either side can take.

parts.name: Armies
parts.text: Yours: 3 from Knight, Bishop, Rook, King. Theirs: 2 from King, Knight, Bishop, Wazir. Lined up like chess.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: Rabbits move yours, once you have set them up; a rabbit inside each of theirs picks its way, by its own mind (intelligence 4). Turns, yours first; every piece of yours moves, then every piece of theirs.

parts.name: Goal
parts.text: Capture them all. A limit of 20 moves.

parts.name: Growth
parts.text: Win rounds to grow your side, up to 6, buying pieces and upgrades with acorns.

parts.name: Difficulty
parts.text: Any difficulty, climbing steadily; each board searched to be won by some setup within 20 turns and balanced.

parts.name: Information
parts.text: Both sides see the whole board. Hints: where theirs can go, shields on guarded pieces, shields on squares you guard, beacons on what can be taken and needles through pinned pieces.
